\chapter{Five Places A Town Has}
\label{ch:lugares-del-pueblo}
\hlchaptermodality{346}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name la escuela, la iglesia, el mercado, la oficina and la estacion, and say why an office was a workshop and a school was spare time.}

Complete ES-C346-estacion: name five buildings a town has and ask where any of them is.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la escuela]{la escuela — the school, which began as spare time}

\label{lesson:ES-C346-escuela}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{heat}, then \emph{age}. (\emph{El calor}; \emph{la edad}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item estudiante — the person who goes there.
  \item el maestro — the person who waits there.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{es-KUE-la}, three beats with the weight on the second. Spanish will not begin a word with \emph{sc-}, so it puts an \emph{e} in front. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la escuela} — \textquotedblleft{}the school.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{skhol\'{\={e}}} did not mean study. It meant \emph{spare time} — the hours a free Athenian was not obliged to spend on work.

What did he do with them? He went and argued in public. So the word for the leisure slid over to the arguing, and then to the group that gathered to argue, and at last to the building they gathered in. Latin borrowed it as \textbf{schola}, and Spanish worked it down to \textbf{escuela}.

English kept the same word twice over: a \textbf{school}, a \textbf{scholar}, a \textbf{scholarship}, and anything \textbf{scholastic}. All four rest on a Greek word for time off.

There is a small piece of Spanish machinery to notice too. Latin \emph{schola} begins \emph{sc-}, and Spanish mouths do not start a word that way, so an \emph{e} grows in front. The same \emph{e} is at the front of \emph{España} and \emph{estudiante}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five places you can point at in a town.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la escuela}
  \item \emph{una escuela}
  \item \emph{¿dónde está la escuela?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{skhol\'{\={e}}} mean in Greek? (Spare time, leisure.) And what English word for a learner comes off it? (Scholar.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la iglesia]{la iglesia — the church, named after the crowd}

\label{lesson:ES-C346-iglesia}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{age}, then \emph{school}. (\emph{La edad}; \emph{la escuela}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la gente — who fills it.
  \item el pueblo — where it usually stands.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{i-GLE-sia}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{g} is hard, as in \emph{gato}, and \emph{-sia} runs together into one beat. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la iglesia} — \textquotedblleft{}the church.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{ekklēsía} was a political word before it was a religious one. It is \textbf{ek}, \emph{out}, plus \textbf{kaleîn}, \emph{to call}: the citizens \textbf{called out} of their houses by a herald, gathered in the open to vote.

Early Christians borrowed that word for their own gatherings, Latin took it as \textbf{ecclēsia}, and Spanish wore it down to \textbf{iglesia}.

So the name belongs to the people, not to the walls. A Spanish speaker saying \emph{la iglesia} is naming a crowd that has been summoned, and only afterwards the roof over it.

English kept the Greek shape in \textbf{ecclesiastical}, and the \emph{kaleîn} half turns up again in \textbf{council} and in a \textbf{calendar}, whose first day was \emph{called out} aloud each month.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two buildings a town has, and both are named for the people inside.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la iglesia}
  \item \emph{una iglesia}
  \item \emph{la iglesia del pueblo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Greek pieces make \emph{ekklēsía}? (\emph{Ek}, out, and \emph{kaleîn}, to call.) And what did it name first — the crowd or the building? (The crowd.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el mercado]{el mercado — the market, and the trade behind mercy}

\label{lesson:ES-C346-mercado}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{school}, then \emph{church}. (\emph{La escuela}; \emph{la iglesia}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la tienda — the smaller thing inside it.
  \item comprar — what you go there to do.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mer-KA-do}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{r} is one tap, and the \emph{d} between vowels is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el mercado} — \textquotedblleft{}the market.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{merx}, \textbf{mercis} meant \emph{goods, wares} — the things themselves. \textbf{Mercātus} was the act of trading them, and then the place where the trading happened.

English took the same root by two roads. Through Latin came \textbf{commerce}, \textbf{mercantile} and \textbf{mercenary}, a soldier who fights for goods rather than for a flag. Through Old French came \textbf{merchant} and \textbf{market}.

The strange one is \textbf{mercy}. Latin \textbf{mercēs} was \emph{the pay owed} for work or wares. In church Latin it drifted: a \emph{mercy} became a payment made where none was owed at all, a wage handed to somebody who had not earned it.

So a market square and an act of mercy come out of the same Latin heap of goods.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three places, and three different reasons a town gathers.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el mercado}
  \item \emph{un mercado grande}
  \item \emph{¿dónde está el mercado?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{merx} mean? (Goods, wares.) And what did \emph{mercēs} mean before it meant mercy? (The pay owed.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la oficina]{la oficina — the office, which used to be a workshop}

\label{lesson:ES-C346-oficina}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{church}, then \emph{market}. (\emph{La iglesia}; \emph{el mercado}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la mesa — what stands in it.
  \item el lugar — the general word this narrows.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{o-fi-SI-na}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft — an \emph{s} across the Americas. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la oficina} — \textquotedblleft{}the office.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had \textbf{opus}, \emph{work}, and \textbf{facere}, \emph{to make}. Stick them together and you get \textbf{opifex}, a \emph{work-maker}, a craftsman. The place he worked was an \textbf{opificīna}.

Four syllables was too many for daily speech, so Latin itself squeezed the middle out and said \textbf{officīna} — a workshop, a forge, a place where something was actually being made.

Spanish kept the workshop sense for centuries. The desk and the paperwork are a late arrival; the word underneath still means the room where the work is done.

English took \textbf{office}, \textbf{officer}, \textbf{official} and \textbf{officious} off the same stem, and kept \textbf{opus} itself for a composer's work. \textbf{Operate}, \textbf{opera} and \textbf{operation} are all \emph{opus} as well.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four places, and one of them is a workshop wearing a suit.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la oficina}
  \item \emph{una oficina nueva}
  \item \emph{la oficina está en la plaza}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin words hide inside \emph{officīna}? (\emph{Opus}, work, and \emph{facere}, to make.) And what was an \emph{officīna} before it was an office? (A workshop.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la estación]{la estación — the station, a place for standing still}

\label{lesson:ES-C346-estacion}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{market}, then \emph{office}. (\emph{El mercado}; \emph{la oficina}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la parada — the smaller stop this outgrew.
  \item estar — the verb hiding at the front of it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{es-ta-SIÓN}, three beats with the weight on the last, which is why it carries a written accent. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la estación} — \textquotedblleft{}the station.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{stāre} meant \emph{to stand}, and a \textbf{statiō} was a \emph{standing-place}: a post where a sentry was set, a road-house where horses were changed, an anchorage where ships stood at rest.

Every later sense grows out of that standing. A railway \textbf{estación} is where a train stands. A radio \textbf{estación} is a fixed point on a dial. And a season of the year is an \emph{estación} too, because the sun appears to stand at the same height for a stretch of weeks.

The same \textbf{stāre} is already in your mouth. \textbf{Estar} is that verb, worn down by two thousand years of use — which is why \emph{estar} is the \emph{to be} you use for where a thing stands rather than what it permanently is.

English is full of it as well: \textbf{station}, \textbf{stationary}, \textbf{status}, \textbf{statue}, \textbf{stable}, \textbf{stance}, \textbf{estate} and \textbf{circumstance}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five places you can name and ask for: a school, a church, a market, an office and a station.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la estación}
  \item \emph{¿dónde está la estación?}
  \item \emph{la estación está en la ciudad}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{stāre} mean? (To stand.) And which everyday Spanish verb is the same word worn down? (\emph{Estar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
